1: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.15–16 — ‘to the discerning, all is suffering’; ‘the suffering yet to come is to be avoided.’ Both texts begin from pain, not from God or the world. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.1.3 — Nārada: ‘I know the mantras but not the Self; I have heard that the knower of the Self crosses sorrow. Take me across.’ Taittirīya Up. 3.1 — ‘desire to know (vijijñāsasva) that from which beings are born.’ Meaning: the question starts with suffering and ends with knowing.
2: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.15 — dispassion toward objects ‘seen or heard of (ānuśravika)’ — Patañjali uses the Kārikā’s word for scriptural reward. Veda: the Veda says this of itself — Muṇḍaka Up. 1.2.7 — ‘unsteady rafts are these forms of sacrifice’; 1.2.12 — ‘the uncreated is not won by what is made’; Muṇḍaka 1.1.5 counts the four Vedas as the lower knowledge. Meaning: the Upaniṣads already ranked knowledge above ritual; the Kārikā builds on that.
3: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.19 sorts the same twenty-five into four levels. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.10–11 orders objects, mind, intellect, the great self (mahat), the unmanifest (avyakta) and the Person (puruṣa) — three Sāṃkhya terms in one verse. Gītā 7.4 lists earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego as ‘my eightfold prakṛti’. Meaning: the twenty-five principles systematise an older Upaniṣadic ladder.
4: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.7 names the same three means — perception, inference, testimony. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — the Self is to be ‘heard, reflected on, and meditated upon’ — testimony, reasoning, direct knowing. Meaning: both schools accept the Veda as testimony, but only as one of three.
5: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.7 again; YS 1.49 adds that yogic insight grasps the particular, which inference and testimony cannot. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.8–9 — the Self is not grasped by one who merely reasons, ‘this insight is not reached by logic.’ Meaning: inference has a place, but a limited one.
6: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.49 — insight reaches what testimony and inference cannot. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.3.12–13 — ‘not by speech, not by mind, not by sight can it be reached. How can it be known except by one who says “It is”?’ Meaning: what is beyond the senses is reached first by testimony, then by inference, and finally by insight.
7: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.25 — yogic sight reaches the subtle, the hidden and the distant — the same causes of non-perception listed here. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.12 — the essence in the banyan seed: ‘you do not see it, yet the great tree stands from it.’ Meaning: not seeing something does not mean it is not there.
8: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.45 — the range of subtle objects ends in the unmarked (prakṛti). Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.13 — salt dissolved in water: unseen but tasted everywhere; Kaṭha Up. 1.3.11 — ‘beyond the great is the unmanifest’. Meaning: the root of nature is known by its effects, like salt by its taste.
9: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.13–14 and 4.12 — the substrate persists; past and future exist in it. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.2.2 — ‘how could being come from non-being?’ — the Upaniṣad’s own argument for satkāryavāda; 6.1.4 — clay alone is real, its forms are names. Meaning: nothing comes from nothing; effects pre-exist in their cause.
10: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.19 — the marked (liṅga) and the unmarked (aliṅga) are this verse’s manifest and unmanifest. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.3.8 — ‘beyond the unmanifest is the Person, pervading and unmarked (aliṅga).’ Meaning: the Kaṭha uses Sāṃkhya’s technical word before Sāṃkhya does.
11: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.15–16 — objects are shared and not dependent on one mind — the ‘common’ (sāmānya) and ‘objective’ here. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 1.10 — ‘pradhāna is perishable; the immortal is imperishable.’ Meaning: nature is real and common; consciousness is its other.
12: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.18 — the seen is luminous, active and stable; YS 2.15 — the guṇas’ conflict makes all experience painful. Veda: Atharvaveda 10.8.43 — ‘the lotus of nine gates covered with three guṇas’; Chāndogya Up. 6.4.1 — red, white and black. Meaning: the three strands of experience have Vedic roots.
13: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.18 (prakāśa, kriyā, sthiti) and 4.14 (one thing from coordinated change). The lamp — wick, oil and flame working together — reappears in YS 4.14’s idea of a unified change. Veda: Gītā 14.6–8 — sattva illumines, rajas drives, tamas binds. Meaning: opposite forces, one purpose.
14: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.13 — all characteristics consist of the guṇas. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — the unborn she-goat ‘producing many offspring like herself’ — effects resembling their cause. Meaning: the unmanifest is known because effects carry its marks.
15: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.45 and 2.19 — limited things point back to the unlimited unmanifest. Veda: Ṛgveda 10.129.1–3 — ‘neither non-being nor being … darkness hidden by darkness’; Chāndogya Up. 6.12 — the seed. Meaning: the variety of the world needs a single source.
16: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.13 and 4.2 — transformation ‘by the in-flow of prakṛti’. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.2.3 — ‘it thought: may I be many’; Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1.7 — ‘as a spider sends out and draws in its thread.’ Meaning: one stuff, changing like water into the shape of each vessel.
17: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.21 and 4.24 — the seen exists for the seer, ‘because it acts in combination’. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — ‘all is dear for the sake of the Self’; Ṛgveda 10.90 names the cosmic Person (puruṣa). Meaning: the world is arranged for a subject.
18: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.22 — the seen ends for one but not for others — which assumes many puruṣas. Veda: here Sāṃkhya differs openly from Ṛgveda 1.164.46 (‘the one being the wise call by many names’) and Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.11 (‘one God in all beings’). The Kārikā argues from different births and deaths; the Upaniṣad from one source. Meaning: an honest disagreement, preserved by both traditions.
19: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.20 — the seer is ‘seeing alone’. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.11 — ‘witness (sākṣī), consciousness, alone (kevala), without guṇas’ — three of this verse’s five terms; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.3.15 — ‘this person is unattached’; Ṛgveda 1.164.20 — the bird that watches without eating. Meaning: the Upaniṣad supplied the vocabulary.
20: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.4, 2.6 and 4.22 — the seer takes on the form of the vṛttis; asmitā is the false identity of seer and seeing. Veda: Gītā 3.27 — ‘actions are done by the guṇas; the one deluded by ego thinks “I am the doer”’; 13.20 — prakṛti is the cause of action, puruṣa of experience. Meaning: we credit the mind with consciousness and the Self with action — both mistakes.
21: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.17 and 2.23 — the conjunction of seer and seen, for knowing each. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 1.9 — ‘two unborn: the knower and the not-knower, the lord and the not-lord’; Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.1 — two birds on one tree. Meaning: the lame man sees, the blind man walks; together they travel, and the trip is for both.
22: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.19 — the levels of the seen. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 2.1 — ‘from the Self came space, from space air, from air fire, from fire water, from water earth’; Muṇḍaka Up. 2.1.3 — from it are born breath, mind, the senses and the elements. Meaning: the Upaniṣads give creation’s order; the Kārikā sets the inner layers above the elements.
23: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.41 — purity brings sattva-śuddhi; YS 1.15 — dispassion; YS 3.45 — power. The Kārikā’s four sattvic forms of buddhi are Yoga’s goals. Veda: Gāyatrī (Ṛgveda 3.62.10) prays for the stirring of dhī, intellect; Kaṭha Up. 1.3.3 — ‘know buddhi as the charioteer.’ Meaning: the intellect is the driver; its quality decides the journey.
24: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.6 — asmitā; YS 4.4 — minds made from asmitā alone. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.4.1 — ‘in the beginning the Self alone … it said first “I am” (aham asmi).’ Meaning: the first act of creation is saying ‘I’.
25: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.47 — mastery of the senses through their source in asmitā. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.4–5 — the threefold division gives mind from food, breath from water, speech from heat. Meaning: senses and elements branch from one ego along different guṇas.
26: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.54–55 — pratyāhāra and mastery of the senses. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.4 — ‘the senses are the horses, objects their roads’; Praśna Up. 4.2 — in sleep all senses become one in the mind. Meaning: ten horses, five for knowing and five for acting.
27: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.53 — the mind fit for concentration. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.3 — ‘mind is the reins’; Śukla Yajurveda 34.1 — ‘that which goes far when awake … may my mind be of auspicious resolve.’ Maitrī Up. 6.34 — ‘mind is the cause of bondage and release.’ Meaning: the mind connects the senses to the self.
28: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.43 — object alone shining — is perception returned to this bare presentation (ālocana). Veda: Kena Up. 1.2 — ‘the eye of the eye’. Meaning: the senses only show; meaning is added inside.
29: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.39–40 — mastery of udāna and samāna; YS 2.49 — prāṇāyāma. Veda: Praśna Up. 3 — prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, udāna described by seat and function; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.5.3 lists the five breaths. Meaning: breath is the common life of mind, ego and intellect.
30: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.20 — the mind cannot know itself and its object at once. The Kārikā says organs act together or in sequence on objects; Yoga adds that self-knowing is never one of those acts. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 3.4.2 — ‘you cannot see the seer of seeing.’ Meaning: perception can be fast, but not self-seeing.
31: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.3 — causes only remove obstacles; nature flows by itself. Veda: Kena Up. 1.1–2 — ‘impelled by whom does the mind go?’ Meaning: the organs cooperate for a purpose they do not own.
32: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.43 — tapas perfects body and senses. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.3–4 — the chariot with its driver, reins and horses. Meaning: thirteen instruments for grasping, holding and showing.
33: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.7 — the last three limbs are ‘inner’ compared to the first five, as here the inner organ is distinguished from the outer ten. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.10 — beyond the senses, mind; beyond mind, intellect. Meaning: the inner organ lives in all three times; the senses only in the present.
34: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.35 and 3.36 — subtle sense perception of non-specific objects. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.11 — subtle appearances in early yoga. Meaning: senses reach both gross and subtle.
35: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.23 — the citta, coloured by seer and seen, grasps all; YS 4.5 — one mind directing many. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.3 — buddhi is the charioteer. Meaning: the senses are doors; the intellect is the keeper.
36: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.17–19 — the mind lights objects but is not self-luminous. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.2.15 — ‘by his light all this shines’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.3.6 — ‘the Self is his light.’ Meaning: the organs are lamps, but their light is borrowed.
37: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.26 and 3.35 — discriminative recognition of sattva and puruṣa. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.12 — ‘seen by subtle seers through a sharp, subtle intellect’; Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.8 — ‘the one of pure sattva sees.’ Meaning: the same intellect that serves enjoyment can see past it.
38: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.44 and 1.44 — subtle and gross elements, mastered in samādhi. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 2.1 — the order of the elements; Chāndogya Up. 6.2–4 — heat, water and food. Meaning: the gross grows from the subtle, and is pleasant, painful or dulling.
39: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.40 and 3.46 — the body seen and perfected. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 8.12.1 — ‘this body is mortal; it is the seat of the immortal, bodiless Self.’ Meaning: subtle body, birth-body, elements — three kinds of specific thing.
40: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.9–10 — vāsanās carried across births, beginningless. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.3 — ‘like a caterpillar … the self reaches the next body’; 4.4.2 — knowledge, deeds and past experience go with it. Meaning: something subtle travels; consciousness itself does not.
41: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.38 — entering another body by loosening the mind’s bond. Veda: Praśna Up. 3.10 — at death, prāṇa joins with the mind and fire and leads the self on. Meaning: the subtle body always needs a support, like a picture needs a wall.
42: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.13 and 4.2 — kinds of birth by karma and the inflow of nature. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.2.7 — ‘some enter a womb, others a stationary thing, according to deeds and knowledge.’ Meaning: like an actor, the subtle body plays many parts.
43: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.1 — powers from birth, herbs, mantra, tapas or samādhi — innate, natural, acquired. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.23 — the Self ‘chooses’ some; Taittirīya Up. 3.2 — others reach it by tapas. Meaning: some qualities are born with us; others are earned.
44: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.14 — joy and pain from merit and demerit; YS 2.24–25 — ignorance binds, its removal frees. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 5.10 — paths up and down by conduct; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — ‘good by good action’; Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.13 — ‘knowing God, one is freed.’ Meaning: virtue lifts, vice lowers, only knowledge frees.
45: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.19 — ‘prakṛtilaya’, absorption into nature — the same word, the same warning: high, but not freedom. YS 3.45 — power gives non-obstruction. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.2.10 — those who stop at merit ‘enjoy heaven, then return.’ Meaning: dispassion without knowledge only parks you in nature.
46: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.3 and 1.30 — afflictions and obstacles; YS 2.42 and 2.29 — contentment and the limbs. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.5 — ‘dwelling in ignorance, thinking themselves wise.’ Meaning: fifty ways the intellect can stall or succeed.
47: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: the five errors are YS 2.3’s five kleśas. Veda: Īśa Up. 9 — ‘blind darkness’. Meaning: Sāṃkhya counts, Yoga treats.
48: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: tamas = avidyā (YS 2.5), moha = asmitā (2.6), mahāmoha = rāga (2.7), tāmisra = dveṣa (2.8), andhatāmisra = abhiniveśa (2.9) — the equation made by Vyāsa and the Sāṃkhya commentators. Veda: Īśa Up. 3 — the ‘worlds covered in blind darkness (andhena tamasāvṛtāḥ)’ — the image behind ‘andhatāmisra’. Meaning: five names for one darkness at five depths.
49: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.30 — nine obstacles, from illness to instability. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.13 lists health and steadiness as early signs of progress — the opposite of incapacity. Meaning: damaged instruments slow the work.
50: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: contrast YS 2.42 — contentment brings ‘unsurpassed happiness’. Sāṃkhya warns against settling for nature, means, time or luck before knowledge. Yoga’s contentment is with circumstance, not with ignorance. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.14 — ‘arise, awake.’ Meaning: don’t mistake comfort for arrival.
51: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.29 — eight limbs; YS 2.44 — svādhyāya; YS 1.33 — friendliness. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.2.12 — ‘go to a teacher’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — hear, reflect, meditate. Meaning: reasoning, teaching and study, together with the end of the three sufferings, good friends and giving.
52: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.10–11 — vāsanās beginningless, held by cause and fruit. Veda: Ṛgveda 10.129.4 — ‘desire arose in the beginning, the first seed of mind.’ Meaning: dispositions and subtle body make each other.
53: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 3.26 — knowledge of the worlds. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.3 and Chāndogya Up. 1.2 — gods and demons; Kaṭha Up. 2.2.7 — beings by karma. Meaning: three orders of embodied life — divine, animal, human.
54: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.22 — differences of intensity; YS 3.26 — realms. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.3.28 — ‘from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light.’ Meaning: sattva above, tamas below, rajas in the middle — where humans stand.
55: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.9 and 2.15 — clinging to life and the suffering of change. Veda: Ṛgveda 7.59.12 — ‘release me from death’; Kaṭha Up. 1.1.26 — ‘these things last only till tomorrow.’ Meaning: as long as the subtle body lasts, so does the pain of decay and death.
56: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.18 — the seen is for experience and release (bhoga-apavarga). Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — ‘for the sake of the Self’. Meaning: nature works for each puruṣa’s freedom, as if for another’s good.
57: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.3 — nature flows by itself once obstacles are removed. Here Yoga adds Īśvara (YS 1.24) where the Kārikā does not need one. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.10 — ‘know prakṛti as māyā and the great Lord as its wielder.’ Meaning: Sāṃkhya says the milk flows by nature; the Upaniṣad says a Lord guides it.
58: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.21 — nature’s essence is for the seer. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.5 — ‘as one desires, so one acts.’ Meaning: just as desire drives action until satisfied, nature acts until release.
59: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.32 — the guṇas’ sequence ends once their purpose is done. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — one unborn ‘leaves her, having enjoyed her.’ Meaning: the dancer stops when the audience has seen.
60: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.21 — the seen exists only for the seer. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — ‘for the sake of the Self’. Meaning: nature serves without being served in return.
61: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.22 and 4.34 — once seen, nature withdraws for that seer. Veda: Kena Up. 3 — the yakṣa vanishes when approached by Indra, leaving the teaching; Kaṭha Up. 2.3.15 — the knot, once cut, does not return. Meaning: nothing is shyer than prakṛti once fully seen.
62: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.20 and 4.18 — puruṣa is unchanging, only appearing to cognise. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.18–19 — ‘it is not born, it does not die … it does not slay, nor is it slain’; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.3.15 — ‘unattached’. Meaning: bondage and release happen in nature; the Self was never caught.
63: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.24 — ignorance causes conjunction; its end ends it. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.2 — grieving from helplessness, freed by seeing the Lord. Meaning: nature ties herself in seven ways and unties herself in one.
64: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.26 — unbroken discriminative recognition; YS 1.48 — truth-bearing insight; YS 4.25 — the end of questions about the self. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.22 — ‘not this, not this’; Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.5 — gained by truth and right knowledge. Meaning: ‘I am not, nothing is mine, no I’ — the Upaniṣad’s negation made personal.
65: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.3 — ‘the seer abides in its own nature’ — the same picture as ‘abiding in itself (svastha), like a spectator’. Veda: Ṛgveda 1.164.20 — the bird that watches without eating; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.23 — ‘calm … he sees the Self in the self.’ Meaning: the watcher stops being drawn into the show.
66: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 2.22 and 4.32 — nature is ‘as if destroyed’ for the freed, though still there. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — one unborn enjoys, the other leaves her; Kaṭha Up. 2.3.14 — desires released. Meaning: contact remains; purpose has gone.
67: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.27–28 and 3.22 — residual saṃskāras and karma already in motion. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.14.2 — ‘delay only until I am released; then I reach home.’ Meaning: the potter’s wheel keeps turning a while after the push stops — the freed sage keeps the body.
68: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 4.34 — kaivalya; YS 2.25 — the absence of conjunction is isolation. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.11 — ‘alone (kevala)’; 6.13 — ‘reached by Sāṃkhya and Yoga’; Muṇḍaka Up. 3.2.8 — rivers entering the ocean. Meaning: both texts end on the same word, drawn from the Upaniṣad.
69: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.25–26 — Īśvara as first teacher; Vyāsa on 1.25 tells the same story of compassionate teaching to Āsuri. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1.1–2 — the chain of teachers from Brahmā; Ṛgveda 10.129.7 — ‘who knows from where this creation came?’ Meaning: a hidden teaching about origin, duration and dissolution.
70: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.1 — ‘anuśāsanam’, teaching passed down; Vyāsa on YS 1.25 quotes Pañcaśikha’s account of Kapila teaching Āsuri. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 5.2 — ‘he who in the beginning bore the seer Kapila.’ Meaning: the Upaniṣad names Sāṃkhya’s founder.
71: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: YS 1.1 — systematising an older teaching. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.6 and 4.6 end with long lineages of teachers. Meaning: like the Upaniṣads, the Kārikā shows its chain of teachers.
72: Yoga ↔ Sāṃkhya: Yoga is sometimes called ‘seśvara Sāṃkhya’, Sāṃkhya with a Lord — the Yoga Sūtras keep the framework this verse summarises and add Īśvara and method. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.13 — ‘the cause reached by Sāṃkhya and Yoga’; Gītā 5.4–5 — ‘the childish say Sāṃkhya and Yoga differ, not the wise; the state reached by Sāṃkhya is also reached by Yoga.’ Meaning: two texts, one aim.
